name: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler
lead: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) filler is a non-absorbable injectable used in dermatology and plastic surgery to add lasting volume to the face: it fills nasolabial folds and atrophic acne scars, and clinicians also use it off-label in the cheeks, chin and jawline. It consists of tiny PMMA microspheres suspended in a carrier gel and is sold in the United States as Bellafill, formerly Artefill and, before that, Artecoll. [5][13][17]

Because the microspheres are not broken down, the body encapsulates each bead in fibrous tissue, and the beads plus that tissue provide the volume; this is why PMMA filler is described as permanent. [2][3][5] The US FDA lists non-absorbable fillers as approved only for the nasolabial folds and for acne scars of the cheek, and states that removal can be difficult or impossible for permanent fillers. [6]

Research includes a pivotal US trial of Artefill in 251 subjects, a randomized acne-scar trial, an open-label pilot of 14 subjects and postmarketing surveillance reports, and reviews of the permanent-filler category. [19][20][18][13] PMMA is the same polymer used in bone cement, dentures, intraocular lenses and other implants. [1][5] In looksmaxxing forums PMMA is discussed mainly in connection with facial implants and permanence, and in bodybuilding forums with injections to enlarge muscles. [8][11][12]
infobox: PMMA microspheres (about 30-40 micrometres) in a collagen or gel carrier [17][14]

paras: PMMA fillers consist of microscopic PMMA beads held in a gel. Artefill and its successor Bellafill contain 20 percent PMMA microspheres by volume, 30 to 40 micrometres across, suspended in 80 percent bovine collagen solution; the collagen serves as a carrier that keeps the beads from clumping and is later replaced by the patient's own connective tissue. [17][14] A 1 mL syringe contains roughly six million microspheres, and the smooth bead surface prompts fibroblasts to encapsulate each one. [14]

Wikipedia describes PMMA filler as injected microspheres in a biological fluid, intended to reduce wrinkles or scars, and Wikipedia's dermal filler article contrasts such particulate scaffolds with degradable fillers, most of which are temporary. [5][23] A review proposes that the filler beneath a crease acts like a splint, allowing the thinned dermis to recover. [14]

The polymer itself dates from the late 1920s and early 1930s: chemists including William Conn, Otto Rohm and Walter Bauer developed it in different laboratories in 1928, Rohm and Haas brought it to market as Plexiglas in 1933, and ICI registered it as Perspex. Harold Ridley implanted the first PMMA intraocular lens at St Thomas' Hospital, London, on 29 November 1949 after noticing that RAF pilots with acrylic splinters from aircraft canopies showed little rejection. PMMA bone cement later became standard in orthopaedics. [5]

As a filler, Artecoll was developed in Europe roughly 20 years before its FDA approval; reviews note that early granuloma reactions were partly attributed to electrostatic charge on the beads, and that purification and manufacturing changes aimed to reduce them. [17][13] A 2018 review dates Arteplast, a PMMA filler developed in 1989, as a step leading to Bellafill. The FDA granted premarket approval to Artefill in 2006, and it was rebranded Bellafill in 2015. [13] PMMA was also widely used in the early 2000s to restore volume in people with HIV-related facial wasting. [5]

The FDA states that non-absorbable fillers are approved only for the nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars, and that unapproved uses include breast, buttock and foot enhancement and injection into the nose, forehead, periorbital area, neck, bone, tendon or muscle. The agency also says injectable silicone is not approved for any aesthetic procedure and that fillers should be given by licensed, trained providers and never self-injected. [6]

A 2023 review of fillers for the chin and jawline covers hyaluronic acid, calcium hydroxylapatite, poly-L-lactic acid and PMMA as options, noting that advantages of fillers include relatively affordable cost and limited recovery time, and that measures are needed to prevent complications. [2] A 2021 systematic review of non-hyaluronic fillers for the midface, covering PMMA, PLLA, calcium hydroxylapatite and autologous fat, identified seven studies and reported that most patients were highly satisfied. [16]
Published and registered human research includes the following.

The pivotal US study of ArteFill enrolled 251 subjects at eight centres who received ArteFill or bovine collagen control in 1,334 wrinkles, with a progress report on 4 to 5-year outcomes published in 2006. [19] The authors describe the product as offering long-lasting and probably permanent augmentation. [19]

A 2010 open-label pilot study of 14 subjects treated atrophic acne scars with subscision followed by Artefill; investigators rated 96 percent of scars as improved at eight months, with no adverse events reported. [18] A double-blind, randomized multicentre trial in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology in 2014 tested suspended PMMA microspheres for atrophic facial acne scars. [20]

A 2018 review reports postmarketing data for 2007 to 2016 in which more than 530,000 Bellafill syringes were distributed worldwide and 11 confirmed granulomas (0.002 percent of syringes) were reported outside clinical trials, and that data on other PMMA fillers are limited and inconsistent. [13] A 2004 review noted that, because the results are permanent, technical errors and incorrect injections also last, and that there has been debate over whether permanent fillers should be used cosmetically. [17] A cross-sectional analysis of adverse events and litigation for injectable fillers was published in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery in 2018. [21]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists a post-approval study of Artefill for nasolabial folds enrolling 1,008 participants, begun in 2007, and a phase 1 study of Artefill for HIV-associated facial lipoatrophy (31 participants, 2013). [3][4] Registered trials of PMMA for gluteal augmentation (137 and 133 participants) are listed as not yet recruiting or of unknown status; gluteal use is outside the FDA's list of approved filler uses. [9][10][6] A 2016 review titled Synthetic Fillers for Facial Rejuvenation and a 2006 overview of permanent and semipermanent fillers cover the wider category. [7][15]

The FDA's general information on dermal fillers lists bruising, redness, swelling and pain as common; nodules or granulomas, infection and allergic reaction as less common; and filler migration, permanent hard nodules, anaphylaxis and vascular injury leading to tissue death, vision loss or stroke as rare. It adds that problems can appear weeks, months or years after injection, and that patients should be allergy-tested before receiving fillers made from animal-derived materials such as bovine collagen. [6]

Because PMMA is not absorbed, complications are not self-limiting in the way they can be with temporary fillers, a point the FDA makes about permanent fillers generally. [6] Wikipedia notes that MMA, the monomer, is an irritant and possible carcinogen although the polymer is biocompatible, and that PMMA bone cement has been linked to cardiopulmonary events in surgery; these concern surgical cement rather than injectable microspheres. [5]

The FDA also warns that fillers bought online may be counterfeit or not approved for use in the United States, and has issued warnings about counterfeit products. Problems can be reported through its MedWatch programme. [6]

On looksmax.org, one user asked whether permanent fillers such as Bellafill cause a reddish colour at the treated places and how they look long term, saying all he knew was that they are permanent. [22] In another thread a user reported that his surgeon proposed PMMA bone cement for cheek implants as a cheaper alternative to PEEK or hydroxyapatite, saying it was biocompatible; the user had heard PMMA was dangerous and asked about side effects, and one reply simply advised against it. [8] That thread concerns bone-cement implants rather than injectable microspheres.

On T Nation, members have said bodybuilder Rich Piana reportedly had PMMA in his arms, and another poster described fear of reduced function from synthol-type injections; these are forum statements and are unverified. [11][12] Wikipedia notes that some bodybuilders illegally inject PMMA to shape muscles. [5]

lore.intro: PMMA is mentioned in forums mainly in connection with implants and muscle-shaping injections, usually with caution rather than endorsement [8][11][12].

claims.claim: PMMA is dangerous to put in the body
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster said he had heard PMMA was dangerous and asked about side effects when offered it as a facial implant material; a reply said not to use it [8].
claims.experts: The FDA lists granulomas, migration and permanent nodules among the risks of fillers and notes permanent fillers can be difficult or impossible to remove [6]; PMMA is also standard in bone cement and dentures [1][5].

claims.claim: Bodybuilders use PMMA injections to enlarge muscles
claims.believers: T Nation members said Rich Piana was rumoured to have PMMA in his arms [11].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that some bodybuilders illegally use PMMA to shape muscles, and the FDA lists injection into muscle as an unapproved filler use [5][6].

claims.claim: Permanent fillers such as Bellafill leave a reddish colour or look worse long term.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster asked whether permanent fillers cause a reddish colour at treated places and how Bellafill looks long term. [22]
claims.experts: The FDA lists redness as a common filler effect and notes that lumps and other problems may appear months or years later; a 2004 review said errors with permanent fillers also last. [6][17]

claims.claim: PMMA filler has a low complication rate when made with modern purification.
claims.believers: Manufacturer-linked and clinician reviews describe purification as a major factor in minimising adverse events. [13]
claims.experts: Postmarketing data cited in a 2018 review reported 11 confirmed granulomas in more than 530,000 syringes, while noting that data on other PMMA fillers are limited. [13]

claims.claim: Permanent fillers can be used to build cheeks, chin or jaw permanently as a cheaper alternative to implants.
claims.believers: A surgeon in a looksmax.org thread reportedly proposed PMMA bone cement for cheek implants as cheaper than PEEK or hydroxyapatite. [8]
claims.experts: The FDA's approved list for non-absorbable fillers is nasolabial folds and acne scars, and a chin and jawline review lists PMMA among several options. [6][2]

card.summary: Permanent filler beads that stay in the face for good; few sources on outcomes, and removal is difficult if problems arise.
card.note: Permanent: the FDA says removal can be difficult or impossible; granulomas and migration can appear years later.

quick.overview:
PMMA filler is made of tiny plastic beads in a gel. The beads are not absorbed, so the body forms tissue around them and the effect is considered permanent. In the US, permanent fillers are approved only for nasolabial folds and cheek acne scars.

In forums it comes up mostly as a warning: users ask about it when a surgeon offers PMMA bone cement for implants, and bodybuilding forums mention it in connection with muscle-shaping injections.
quick.mechanism: The microspheres act as a scaffold that the body cannot break down; surrounding tissue forms fibrous collagen around them, which adds volume.
quick.risks: The FDA lists lumps, granulomas, infection, migration, permanent hard nodules and rare vascular injury (including blindness) as possible filler complications, some appearing years later. Removal can be difficult or impossible. Use in the buttocks, muscles or other unapproved sites is not sanctioned.

chain: Microspheres in a gel are injected into the dermis or subcutaneous tissue
The body forms fibrous tissue around each bead
A lasting increase in volume that softens folds, fills acne scars and lifts contours
angle.text: PMMA filler is used by physicians to fill nasolabial folds and depressed acne scars, and off-label to build cheek, chin or jaw contours. Its appeal is that the result is intended to be permanent rather than repeated every year or so.
